history.heading: Three atolls
paragraphs: Tokelau consists of three small coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, in the South Pacific north of Samoa. They were settled by Polynesians around 1,000 years ago. In the 1860s Peruvian slave traders kidnapped many of the men, devastating the population.

Tokelau became a British protectorate in 1889 and was transferred to New Zealand in 1925. In referendums in 2006 and 2007, Tokelauans narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for self-government in free association with New Zealand.

culture.heading: Communal life
paragraphs: About 1,500 people live on the atolls, and many more Tokelauans live in New Zealand. Tokelauan and English are spoken. Most people are Christian. Life is organised communally by village councils of elders (taupulega), and resources such as fish are shared through the traditional inati system. Fatele dancing is a celebrated tradition.

politics.heading: New Zealand territory
paragraphs: Tokelau is a non-self-governing territory of New Zealand. It has its own General Fono (parliament) and a rotating head of government. Tokelauans are New Zealand citizens. There is no capital; each atoll has its own administration.

economy.heading: Small and sustainable
paragraphs: The economy relies on New Zealand aid, fishing licences, and revenue from the .tk internet domain. Tokelau was one of the first places in the world to run entirely on solar power, from 2012. Rising sea levels threaten the low-lying atolls. The currency is the New Zealand dollar.
